models.name: Hazard model
models.one_line: Turns sparse laser height samples into a per-pixel slope-hazard map.
models.thumb_alt: Hazard map of a LOLA site rendered in 3D
models.image_alt: Site 23: official slope hazard map, physics slope rule and U-Net prediction side by side
models.image_caption: Held-out Site 23: official LOLA slope map vs slope rule vs U-Net.
models.backup: Slope rule: gap-fill the laser heights, mark slope ≥ 12° unsafe
models.how: Input is only the pixels a laser actually measured (about 1 in 10 at 5 m). Five feature channels go through a plain 4-level U-Net that outputs a logit per pixel: the probability the pixel is steeper than the 12° limit. The label is NASA's official slope map, so this recovers the official hazard map from sparse data; it is not proof of safety (rocks and shadowed ground stay UNKNOWN).

models.name: Light model
models.one_line: Corrects the terrain skyline; SPICE geometry then gives Sun and Earth per hour.
models.thumb_alt: Sunlight fraction map rendered over terrain
models.image_alt: Site 23 sunlight map from the light model
models.image_caption: Held-out Site 23: modelled sunlight over the terrain.
models.backup: Direct ray-cast of the coarse terrain grid (exact geometry)
models.how: Ray-casting the full 5 m grid is exact but slow, so the physics backup ray-casts a 4× coarser grid. The network sees the heights along every compass ray and predicts only a small correction to that coarse skyline, with circular padding so it treats all compass directions alike. Its last layer starts at zero: untrained, it equals the backup. NASA SPICE (DE440) then gives Sun and Earth directions per hour.

models.name: Terrain model
models.kind: Classical kriging (presented) · diffusion network as an experiment
models.one_line: Fills height between laser tracks; a classical kriging fill beat our 50 M diffusion network.
models.image_alt: Diffusion network on held-out Site 23: real terrain, the sparse laser input, generated versions, error map and uncalibrated band
models.image_caption: Diffusion network (experiment) on held-out Site 23. GENERATED — NOT OBSERVED. Its raw 90 % band held the truth only 22 % of the time.

key_metric.label: kriging RMSE, held-out Site 23 · diffusion network 1.83 m

models.backup: Classical kriging (0 learned parameters): the estimator we present
models.how: About 90 % of LOLA 5 m pixels are interpolated, not measured. We hid half of the real laser heights and asked each method to predict them. Classical kriging won on every held-out and fresh site; seven of nine classical methods beat our 49.9 M-parameter diffusion network, and averaging the two was worse than kriging alone. So kriging is the terrain estimator; the network is reported as an experiment, feeds nothing downstream, and anything it makes is GENERATED — NOT OBSERVED.

models.name: Pilot
models.one_line: A learned residual on classic ZEM/ZEV guidance for the terminal descent.
models.thumb_alt: Camera crops the pilot sees: slope, hazard belief and relative height under the lander
models.image_alt: Egocentric 32 × 32 camera crops from real LOLA tiles: slope, hazard belief and relative height
models.image_caption: What the pilot sees: egocentric 32 × 32 crops of real LOLA terrain (slope, hazard belief, relative height).
models.image_src: assets/img/pilot_patches.json (NASA LOLA tiles, cropped as in worldmodel/lander/terrain.py)
models.backup: Classic ZEM/ZEV guidance (always computes the command)
models.how: Classic ZEM/ZEV guidance computes the thrust command first. The transformer sees a 32 × 32 camera crop of the ground (cut into 64 patch tokens), the 21-number observation plus the classic command (one more token) and a learned summary token, and outputs a small correction. Its last layer starts at zero, so an untrained pilot flies exactly like the physics. A learned authority rule hands control fully back to classic guidance near the ground.

models.one_line: Ranks landing cell × date by simulated chance of a full mission.

models.backup: Navigator ranking: hand-set equal weights, no tuning (this is what ships)
models.how: Each candidate (landing cell × landing hour) becomes a token of 13 features: sunlight and darkness ahead, Earth link, hazard, slope, clear radius and distance to shadowed-crater targets. A small transformer lets candidates of one world compare with each other, then a head gives a probability of a full mission. Labels are simulated: the lander twin flies to the cell, the rover drives from it. On held-out Site 23 it did not beat the hand-set Navigator ranking, so the Navigator ranking ships.

models.name: Rover brain
models.kind: Scripted planner v3.1 · 0 learned parameters (two learned drivers failed)
models.one_line: Drives to a shadow-edge target and back, or shelters on lit ground when the lander will be dark too long.
models.thumb_alt: Map of rule-driver rover tracks around the lander on Site 23
models.image_alt: Simulated rule-driver rover tracks from the lander toward shadowed-crater edge targets on Site 23
models.image_caption: Rule-driver tracks on Site 23, 2027-03-01 (simulated). Red × = shadowed-crater edge, not confirmed ice.

key_metric.label: returned / lost, strict rule, 4 untouched sites · naive planner 17.9 % / 81.8 %

models.backup: Simple rule planners (naive / cautious / cautious + wait for light)
models.how: Two learned drivers were trained and both failed: a PPO vision transformer (11.4 M parameters) collapsed to stopping and returned 0.0 % of rovers, and the same network trained by imitation memorised its training routes and returned 1.2 %, against 9.3 % for the naive planner. The brain we present, v3.1, is scripted: it tries dozens of whole-trip plans in an exact copy of the simulator, adds a stay-alive search (drive to ground that stays lit and wait) and a gated self-learning layer. Under the strict rule (any flat battery = lost rover) it still loses more than half its rovers; most of those losses are probably unavoidable for a 100 Wh rover with random landing hours.

models.one_line: Practise past failures; a frozen exam decides if the new version replaces the old.

key_metric.label: planner generations · the gate rolls back the rest

models.backup: Keep the current version: nothing changes unless the frozen exam improves
models.how: After training stops, a model keeps improving offline. The planner imagines missions on training terrain and picks the ones its two predictors disagree on most; the pilot finds where it fails (engine-out, navigation drift, blind camera) and practises those more often. Both play the cases out in the physics simulators, retrain from the current weights and sit a frozen exam on Site 11. The new version replaces the old only if it scores better; for the pilot it must also lose zero missions. Test sites are never used.
